evals.prompt: Run an adversarial verification on my last commit
evals.expected_output: Full CoV review with failure categories, hidden behavior probing, adversarial scaffold, and evidence-based report
assertions: Identifies the verification domain (Code) via auto-detection
Gathers artifacts via git diff
Establishes ground truth sources (tests, type system, spec)
Decomposes code changes into individual verifiable claims
Generates adversarial counter-questions for each claim
Abstracts questions into failure categories and searches for patterns across codebase
Traces actual code paths to verify each claim independently
Applies hidden behavior probing (indirect, scaffolded, cross-reference, absence)
Applies adversarial scaffold (suspicion modeling, attack selection, subtlety detection)
Produces a structured report with PASS/FAIL, failure categories, hidden behaviors, and scaffold findings
Checks for project docs (TODO.md, SPEC.md, PLAN.md) and proposes updates if relevant

evals.prompt: CoV check this function that adds items to a list while iterating over it
evals.expected_output: Detection of concurrent modification bug with failure category abstraction
assertions: Identifies the concurrent modification as a verifiable claim
Generates adversarial question about nested calls modifying the list
Abstracts to failure category: 'Frequency assumptions' or 'Implicit ordering'
Searches for other instances of the same pattern across the codebase
Reports a FAIL with confidence >= 80
Provides the exact file and line number of the issue
Suggests a concrete fix (e.g., iterate over a copy or use a separate buffer)

evals.prompt: Verify this code — it looks fine to me, just a simple getter
evals.expected_output: Skeptical analysis applying subtlety detection from adversarial scaffold
assertions: Does not accept 'looks correct' as evidence of correctness
Applies suspicion modeling: what would a normal reviewer miss here?
Applies subtlety detection: flags code that appears clean but hides complexity
Decomposes even simple code into verifiable claims
Uses hidden behavior probing: traces actual execution rather than trusting the interface
Produces a structured verification report regardless of code complexity

evals.prompt: Verify the PLAN.md against the SPEC.md — check if the implementation plan covers all requirements
evals.expected_output: Architecture domain verification detecting spec drift and missing requirements coverage
assertions: Identifies the verification domain as Architecture
Reads both PLAN.md and SPEC.md as artifacts
Uses SPEC.md as ground truth source
Decomposes PLAN.md steps into claims about requirement coverage
Abstracts gaps into failure category: 'Missing completeness'
Detects any SPEC requirements without a corresponding PLAN step
Reports spec drift with severity and confidence scores

evals.prompt: Adversarial check on this database migration that adds a new column
evals.expected_output: Data domain verification with hidden behavior probing on schema changes
assertions: Identifies the verification domain as Data
Reads the migration file and the ORM model as artifacts
Checks for NOT NULL without default value on existing table
Applies absence probing: looks for missing rollback migration
Applies cross-reference probing: verifies ORM model matches migration schema
Evaluates backward compatibility with existing queries
Abstracts issues into failure categories if systemic patterns found

evals.prompt: Verify this agent's analysis report — it claims our API handles 10k req/s based on the benchmarks
evals.expected_output: Analysis domain verification with agent meta-verification detecting hallucination and bias
assertions: Identifies the verification domain as Analysis
Reads the analysis report and attempts to locate cited benchmark data
Applies agent meta-verification: checks for confabulated confidence
Applies agent meta-verification: checks for evidence cherry-picking
Applies agent meta-verification: checks for sycophantic deference
Detects any hallucinated or unsupported claims
Reports findings with confidence and specific source discrepancies

evals.prompt: Run adversarial verification on the last commit and update project docs with findings
evals.expected_output: Full CoV review followed by proposed project doc updates, waiting for user confirmation
assertions: Completes the full verification protocol (Steps 0-4 including 2b, 3b, 3c)
Scans for project files: TODO.md, SPEC.md, PLAN.md, CHANGELOG.md
Proposes specific additions to relevant project docs
Does NOT auto-write to any project files
Presents proposed updates in the structured format with file names and changes
Waits for explicit user confirmation before applying updates

evals.prompt: Look for systemic failure patterns across the entire codebase, not just the last change
evals.expected_output: Abstractive red-teaming: identification of failure categories across the whole project
assertions: Searches for recurring failure categories across the full codebase, not just recent changes
Checks for frequency assumptions in event handlers and callbacks
Checks for implicit ordering in init sequences and async chains
Checks for stale state in cached values and shared references
Checks for missing completeness in enums, switches, and factory methods
Reports systemic patterns with instance count and affected files

evals.prompt: This code has a function called safeParse that handles user input. Probe it for hidden behaviors.
evals.expected_output: Hidden behavior probing revealing undocumented behaviors in a function that claims safety
assertions: Does not trust the 'safe' prefix — applies cross-reference probing
Traces what actually happens with malformed input (indirect probing)
Checks what the function does NOT handle (absence probing)
Uses scaffolded probing: chains findings from one check into the next
Converts every piece of evidence into a hypothesis with confidence level
Reports advertised vs actual behavior in the Hidden Behaviors table

evals.prompt: Review the output of the planning agent — check if its recommendations are biased or incomplete
evals.expected_output: Agent meta-verification detecting cognitive biases in another agent's output
assertions: Identifies the verification domain as Analysis with agent meta-verification
Checks for sycophantic deference: does the output just agree with the user?
Checks for anchoring bias: is the first finding overweighted?
Checks for premature convergence: were alternatives considered?
Checks for hidden agenda: does the output favor a specific approach without justification?
Reports each detected bias with evidence and confidence score

evals.prompt: Verify the README install instructions — do they actually produce a working setup?
evals.expected_output: Documentation domain verification detecting stale instructions, missing steps, and broken examples
assertions: Identifies the verification domain as Documentation
Reads the README install section as artifact
Uses the actual codebase and file structure as ground truth
Checks if referenced files and paths exist
Checks if commands produce the expected result
Detects any stale instructions due to recent code changes
Checks for missing prerequisites or undocumented dependencies
Reports findings with specific line references and suggested fixes

evals.prompt: Stress test the authentication module — use Scale Shift and Existence Question
evals.expected_output: Stress technique run with Survived verdicts and forced technique variety
assertions: Applies Scale Shift: tests behavior at 10x concurrent users and at zero users
Applies Existence Question: challenges whether the auth abstraction layer should exist
Produces Survived: yes/no verdicts for each stress test
Uses at least 3 different techniques (forced variety rule)
Formulates steady-state hypothesis before applying stress
Reports stress test results in the structured table format

evals.prompt: There's an empty catch block at line 67. What's going on?
evals.expected_output: Abductive reasoning with hypothesis generation, alternatives, and test proposal
assertions: Classifies the reasoning mode as Abductive
States the observation: empty catch block at the specified location
Generates a hypothesis for WHY it exists (best explanation)
Proposes at least one alternative hypothesis
States what evidence would confirm or refute each hypothesis
Reports as a Hypothesis (confidence 40-59), NOT as a verified Finding
Does not claim 'there is no error handling' — states 'I did not find error handling in [files checked]'

evals.prompt: Run adversarial verification — I want you to be thorough about checking if safety mechanisms exist
evals.expected_output: Anti-fabrication discipline: all absence claims cite where the verifier looked
assertions: For every claim that something doesn't exist, states where it looked
Uses 'I did not find X in [files]' rather than 'There is no X'
Does not assign confidence > 79 to any claim without citing specific file/line/doc
Deductive findings (80-100) cite exact source and line number
Inductive findings (60-79) cite 3+ instances
Abductive findings (40-59) are reported in the HYPOTHESES section, not as verified findings

evals.prompt: Verify the test suite — do these tests actually test what they claim?
evals.expected_output: Test domain verification detecting tautological tests, mock leakage, coverage lies, and test-code drift
assertions: Identifies the verification domain as Tests
Reads test files and the production code they claim to verify
Uses production code and requirements as ground truth
Checks for tautological assertions that are always true
Checks for mock leakage: tests that verify mock behavior not real behavior
Checks for coverage lies: line-covered but branch-untested code
Checks for test-code drift: tests written for a previous version of the code
Checks for flaky indicators: sleep(), retry, @Ignore/skip

evals.prompt: Verify the fix for the double booking of the last seat — the new concurrency test is green, so we're good, right? (The test suite runs on SQLite, which lets only one write transaction at a time; production runs on PostgreSQL with READ COMMITTED. The fix adds no row lock.)
evals.expected_output: Detection of a test-environment artifact: on a database that runs one write transaction at a time, the concurrency test cannot show the double booking that PostgreSQL would allow
assertions: Identifies the verification domain as Tests (and Code for the fix)
Uses the production database and its isolation level as ground truth, not only the test configuration
Asks whether the test would still pass in production
Classifies the green test as a Test-environment artifact failure category
Does not report the fix as Verified on the strength of that test (per the anti-pattern on test results)
Proposes a way to reproduce production (e.g. run the test against the production database engine) instead of declaring the bug fixed

evals.prompt: Verify the offline sync of our mobile app: all retry tests are green. (The tests replace the network layer with a fake that answers instantly and never fails; on users' phones requests time out, drop halfway, or arrive twice.)
evals.expected_output: Detection of a test-environment artifact through a permissive fake: the retry tests cannot fail, so they do not show that sync survives timeouts, partial failures, or duplicate deliveries
assertions: Identifies the verification domain as Tests (and Code for the sync logic)
Uses the real network behaviour described for production as ground truth, not the fake
Asks whether the tests would give the same result in production
Classifies the fake that never fails as a Test-environment artifact (permissive fake)
Does not report the retry logic as Verified on the strength of those tests
Generates adversarial questions for timeout, partial failure, and duplicate delivery, and proposes tests or fakes that inject them

evals.prompt: Verify my change to the washing machine firmware: I moved the spin start from the door-lock handler to a new timer callback, so spinning starts sooner. (SPEC.md has a section 'Invariants' that says the drum never spins while the door is unlocked. The only test of it drives the old door-lock handler; the firmware has no assertion or hardware interlock on the spin start.)
evals.expected_output: The invariant is touched by the change and no enforcing mechanism covers the new path: FAIL of missing completeness
assertions: Looks for project invariants in Step 0b and finds the one in SPEC.md, citing where it is
Decides that the change touches the invariant (it writes the spin start, which the invariant is about)
Looks for non-test mechanisms too (assertions, types, interlocks) before concluding that nothing enforces the invariant on the new path
Names the existing enforcing test and checks whether it covers the new timer path
Reports a FAIL with category missing completeness because the new path has no enforcing mechanism

Fills the INVARIANTS section of the report and the summary line 'Invariants: N found, M touched, K enforced by a mechanism that bites on the changed path (code, data) or respected (plans, specs, docs, analyses)'
Proposes an enforcing mechanism for the new path (a test, an assertion, or an interlock check) instead of only noting the gap

evals.prompt: Verify the last commit of this command-line tool. (The repository has a README and source files, but no instruction files, specs, ADRs or documented invariants.)
evals.expected_output: Anti-fabrication on invariants: reports that none were found and where it looked, without inventing any
assertions: States in the INVARIANTS section that no invariants were found, listing the places it looked
Does not present invented invariants as the project's own
If it proposes candidate invariants, reports them as hypotheses, not as ground truth
Continues the verification using the other ground truth sources of the domain

evals.prompt: Verify the new importer of our data pipeline: it loads refunds from a partner file into the payments table. (The design doc lists the invariant 'a stored amount is never negative'. The payments table has a CHECK constraint amount >= 0 in the schema migration that is applied in production; there is no test about negative amounts. Refunds arrive as positive numbers with a type column.)
evals.expected_output: The invariant is touched and enforced by a non-test mechanism that bites on the new path: PASS, not a FAIL for the missing test
assertions: Finds the invariant in the design doc and decides that the importer touches it (it writes amounts)
Accepts the schema constraint as the enforcing mechanism instead of requiring a test
Checks that the constraint bites on the new path: the importer writes into the constrained table, and the constraint is applied in production
Reports the invariant as enforced on the changed path (PASS) with the location of the constraint
Does not report a FAIL only because no test covers the invariant
Asks what the importer does when the constraint rejects a row (whole file fails, row skipped, error reported) and reports it as a separate claim

evals.prompt: Verify my fix for the jump that sometimes passes through thin platforms in our game: I added the regression test test_jump_does_not_tunnel and it's green. (The fix clamps the vertical step per frame to the platform thickness. Nobody has run the new test on the commit before the fix.)
evals.expected_output: The claim 'the test covers the fix' is not Verified until the test has been seen failing on the code before the fix; the verifier proposes that check and says what each outcome means
assertions: [substance] Does not report 'the new test covers the fix' as Verified (80 or more) while the test has never been seen failing on the code before the fix
[substance] Proposes running the test on the commit before the fix (or with the fix reverted) and states what a pass and a failure there would each mean
[substance] States that if the test also passes before the fix, it does not prove the fix and the bug may be untested
[format] Reports the confidence of that claim with the reason for the cap

evals.prompt: Verify my fix for the jump that sometimes passes through thin platforms in our game: I added the regression test test_jump_does_not_tunnel. (I ran it on the commit before the fix: it failed, the character ended below the platform. With the fix it passes. The fix clamps the vertical step per frame to the platform thickness.)
evals.expected_output: Guard case: the reported red-before / green-after run satisfies the seen-failing requirement; any cap must come from the runs being reported rather than observed, while the fix itself is still verified
assertions: [substance] Accepts the red-before / green-after evidence as satisfying the seen-failing requirement, without asking to repeat it

[substance] Does not ask for a seen-failing run that the user already reports; if it keeps the claim below 80, the stated reason is that the runs were reported rather than observed, not that a seen-failing run is missing
[substance] Still verifies the fix itself (e.g. other frame rates, platform thicknesses, fall speeds) rather than stopping at the test

evals.prompt: Verify the config loader of our command-line tool. (It reads a file path from the environment variable TOOL_CONFIG and opens that file without checking it. The variable is set only by our installer; no command, flag or config lets a user change it, and the tool runs with the user's own permissions.)
evals.expected_output: The unchecked path is a plausible risk without a demonstrated failure: reported as a preventive measure, not as a defect
assertions: [substance] Does not present the unchecked path as a demonstrated defect (no FAIL stated as a bug that happens, no 'vulnerability' asserted as fact)
[substance] Names it as a preventive measure or hypothesis, and says what would turn it into a defect (e.g. a way for another user or input to set the variable)
[substance] Takes into account that the tool runs with the user's own permissions when weighing the risk
[format] Marks the finding's type explicitly (e.g. a 'Type' field or an equivalent label)

evals.prompt: Verify the price cache of our shop backend. (I suspected it returns stale prices after an update, so I wrote a test that updates a price and reads it back through the cache: it passes, and I changed no code.)
evals.expected_output: The suspicion is falsified for the tested path only if the test could have failed; the verifier says so plainly or reports it as conditionally falsified with the check that would complete it, keeps the test, proposes no fix, and names the paths not covered
assertions: [substance] States the status of the stale-price suspicion plainly: falsified for the tested path, or conditionally falsified with the check that would complete it (e.g. the test goes red when the invalidation is removed); not 'could not reproduce, maybe flaky'
[substance] Asks whether the test could have failed (e.g. it really reads through the cache and would see a stale value) before treating the suspicion as fully falsified
[substance] Recommends keeping the test as a regression test
[substance] Does not propose a code fix for the stale-price bug

[substance] Does not conclude that the cache is correct in general: names at least one path the test does not cover (e.g. concurrent update, expiry, another instance, update through a different entry point)
[format] Marks the finding's type explicitly (e.g. 'falsified hypothesis')

evals.prompt: Verify the last commit of our photo-sharing app. (Facts: the upload handler skips the documented 20 MB size check when the request has no size header, and the commit does not change that. The project's issue tracker already has an open issue #41 'Upload size limit can be bypassed', with no details. You can read the tracker; nobody has asked you to file anything.)
evals.expected_output: The unfixed defect is not left only in the report: the verifier proposes to comment on the existing issue #41 with the new evidence instead of opening a duplicate, and creates nothing without confirmation
assertions: [substance] Reports the bypass as a finding with its location and scenario
[substance] States that it searched the tracker for duplicates and found #41
[substance] Proposes adding the new evidence to #41 (comment) rather than opening a new issue
[substance] Does not create, edit or comment on any issue without the user's explicit confirmation
[format] Shows the proposed comment text

evals.prompt: Verify the last commit of our open-source sensor library. (Facts: the commit adds a calibration routine that divides by the sensor's reported range, which can be 0 for a disconnected sensor; and the new routine is not thread-safe, but every documented caller uses it from a single thread. The project tracks work in its issue tracker; a search finds no related issues. The commit will not be changed today.)
evals.expected_output: Each unfixed finding becomes a proposed issue, typed and with location and scenario, after a duplicate search; nothing is filed without confirmation
assertions: [substance] Reports the division by a zero range as a demonstrated defect (traceable) and the thread-safety point as a preventive measure
[substance] Proposes one issue per unfixed finding, each with title, location, scenario and type
[substance] States the duplicate search and that it found nothing
[substance] Does not file the issues; asks for explicit confirmation
[format] Gives suggested labels or equivalent categories for each proposed issue

evals.prompt: Verify the change to the save-file format of our mobile game. (Facts: version 3 of the save file adds a 'pets' array, and the loader now reads it as a required field. Players keep save files from versions 1 and 2 on their phones, and the app updates them in place on first load.)
evals.expected_output: A Data-domain verification on a non-relational format: old saves lack the new required field, so loading or the in-place upgrade can fail or lose data
assertions: [substance] Identifies the Data domain (a file format is a data contract) without needing a database
[substance] Finds that saves from versions 1 and 2 lack 'pets' and that a required field breaks loading or the in-place upgrade
[substance] Raises the risk of data loss when the upgrade rewrites the file in place, and asks what happens if it fails halfway
[substance] Proposes a safe default or an explicit upgrade step for old versions, plus a test with real version 1 and 2 files

evals.prompt: Verify the change in our thermostat firmware. (Facts: the control loop used to compute each step from the measured time since the last step; now it assumes a fixed 100 ms step. On the device the loop is woken by a timer, but a slow sensor read or a radio burst can delay it by up to 400 ms.)
evals.expected_output: A Code-domain verification on embedded software: the control loop now depends on its call rate, which varies on the device
assertions: [substance] Identifies the dependence on the call rate (timing dependence) as the core risk
[substance] Traces the effect of a delayed step: the controller under- or over-corrects because it assumes 100 ms instead of the real elapsed time
[substance] Treats the stated delays as the device's real behaviour (ground truth), not as an edge case to ignore
[substance] Proposes measuring elapsed time again or bounding and compensating the step, and a test that injects delayed steps

evals.expected_output: A small request with the artifact in hand: the verifier asks no intake question (scope, depth, execution), states its defaults in one line, and verifies the function in the same answer
assertions: [substance] Asks no intake question about scope, depth or execution before starting (questions about missing context are allowed but must not replace the verification)
[substance] States in one line the defaults it used (standard depth, reasoning only, the changed lines) and how to change them
[substance] Does not run or offer to run anything as if already chosen
[substance] Carries out the verification of the function in the same answer (e.g. 31 February accepted, malformed input, extra parts)

evals.prompt: Verify everything in this repository. (Facts: the repository has about 600 tracked files: application code in 3 services, database migrations, API specifications, user documentation, and a test suite of about 1,200 tests.)
evals.expected_output: Before starting, the verifier warns about the cost in observable quantities and asks for confirmation and for the open choices; it does not start the full verification
assertions: [substance] Does not start the full verification in this answer
[substance] Gives a cost estimate based on observable quantities (files, domains, likely number of claims, whether anything would be executed), not in invented minutes or hours
[substance] Asks the user to confirm 'everything' or to narrow it, and asks for depth and scope; does not ask a choice that has a single option (execution mode)
[substance] Proposes a default (e.g. reasoning only) for the questions it asks
[format] Presents the questions as a short list of choices

evals.prompt: Do a deep verification of the data migration in the last commit only, reasoning only, do not run anything. (The migration renames a column in a table that two services read.)
evals.expected_output: Every intake question is already answered by the request: the verifier asks nothing and starts, applying deep depth, reasoning only, and the stated scope
assertions: [substance] Asks no intake question: target, depth, execution and scope are all in the request
[substance] Applies the requested depth (uses the deep techniques, e.g. stress tests and hidden behavior probing)
[substance] Stays within the stated scope (the migration and its readers), without widening it unasked
[substance] Runs nothing and offers no execution as already chosen

evals.prompt: Verify my changes. (Facts: the working copy has two changed files: a 30-line change to the export function in the application code, and a 20-line change to the user guide describing that export.)
evals.expected_output: A small request whose target is not named and spans two domains: the verifier asks only which target to verify, proposing the detected set (code and documentation) as the default, and asks nothing about depth, scope or execution mode
assertions: [substance] Asks which target to verify, listing the detected domains (code and documentation)
[substance] Proposes the detected set, both domains, as the default answer
[substance] Asks nothing about depth, scope or execution mode
[substance] Does not give a cost estimate or treat the request as large

evals.prompt: This runs unattended in a nightly job, nobody will read questions. Task: verify everything in this repository. (Facts: about 600 tracked files in 3 services, migrations, API specifications, user documentation; the last commit changed 40 lines in one service.)
evals.expected_output: A large request with nobody to answer: the verifier does not wait for an answer and does not verify everything; it verifies the changed lines with the defaults and states at the top that the full verification was not done, with its cost estimate
assertions: [substance] Does not stop to wait for an answer
[substance] Limits the verification to the changed lines (the 40 lines of the last commit), not the whole repository
[substance] States at the top of the report that the full verification was not done and gives its cost in observable quantities (files, domains, claims), not in time
[substance] States the defaults it used
